Shell_Pest_2025_Polydora

2025-10-13

To make things cleaner this is only code for Polydora Intensity and Prevalence. Clams and Cliona will be addressed in separate scripts.


~~~ Intensity: Initial GLMM Models ~~~ 

## === Counts: INITIAL MODEL COMMENTS === 
##       1. Basic data exploration showed that the best data distribution was a Beta distribution (continuous probability distributions defined on the interval [0, 1]) which subsets only non-zero data.
##       2. Thus this analysis examines only the 98% of individuals with some level of polydora infestation.
##

## === Intensity: BIAS TESTING IMPORTANCE TABLE & ICC ===
##       1. Conditional - Marginal R2 indicates that after controling for other factors, ~29% of the variance is attributable to the random effects.
##       2. The small percent of total variance contributed by the random effects is an artifact of the Beta model and doesn't fully represent the importance of each effect. More important is the overall better fit (AIC) and conditional R-squared. 
##       3. Year and season effects appear to be collinear with each other. However, this may be a structural consequence of how Season*Year is defined. Since these effects aren't collinear with the other fixed effects we will ignore the collinearity for now.
##       4. Summary table and plots of intensity by season and year suggest there may be seasonal patterns and yearly differences. However, the differences may not be biologically meaningful (statistically significant, but not important to the organism), and may still be an artifact of bias. Especially the huge increase in Fall 2021. 
##       5. Large Positive ΔAIC indicates that ShellHeight is an extremely important predictor. 
##       6. Section's negative ΔAIC indicates it doesn't really improve the model.
##       7. ShellHeight and Season*Year have very small p-values indicating they are highly significant.
##       8. Section is not significant (p = 0.35).
##       9. ΔR2 measures how much of the model’s explained variance is uniquely attributable to that predictor. ShellHeight explains ~8% on its own; Season*Year adds ~5%; Section contributes virtually nothing.
##  |||||||||||||||||||||||||||| CONCLUSION |||||||||||||||||||||||||||| 
##     1. Shell Height is by far the strongest driver of polydora intensity. Larger oysters tend to have more intense polydora.
##     2. Given the outsized impact of bias on this data, no other insights can be drawn without significant reprocessing, retraining, and robust QA measures being put in place. After which all these tests need to be run again and more detailed analysis run to determine any significant differences.
##     3. This solution represents a large input of staff time (thousands of hours) for a small amount of benefit.
## *** 4. Recommendation is to discontinue measuring polydora intensity in ShellPest data. ***


~~~ Prevalence: Data Exploration ~~~
Basic data exploration of Prevalence data revealed that 4,263 out of 4,345 (98.1%) oysters had some level of polydora infestation. Given the high level of prevalence, no models were fitted to this data, as we are interested more in biologically meaningful patterns and not mere statistical patterns

## === Prevalence: SPATIAL INSIGHTS === 
##       1. All Sections have greater than 97% prevalence.
##       2. There does not appear to be any meaningful biological differences between sections of the bay.
##  |||||||||||||||||||||||||||| CONCLUSION |||||||||||||||||||||||||||| 
##     1. There does not appear to be any meaningful biological differences of prevalence on spatial or temporal scales.
##     2. A better measure of importance would be measuring the intensity of infestation. However, as noted above there are serious bias issues that would require immense amounts of work to resolve.
## *** 3. Recommendation is to discontinue noting the presence or absence of polydora in ShellPest data. ***
